title: How to composite AI generated images together so they actually match?
author: emilrueh
selftext:
I'm building a game that generates all assets in 2D during play. Objects have to be separable from the scene so they can be clicked and picked up without having to redraw the background every time. Everything runs on FLUX.2 klein 4B with a LoRA trained on an illustrator's style.

The workflow:

1. Generate an empty location as background.
2. A vision model outlines foreground, middle and background, and code turns that into a color map of the three planes.
3. Generate objects on white on a 512 canvas and animate them.
4. The vision model points at a spot in the background for each object by outputting pixel coordinates.
5. The object's size is its class (tiny, small, medium, large, huge) times the factor of the plane at that spot, e.g. a torch (small) is 100 px, so in the middle plane (0.75) it's drawn at 75 px.
6. Scale the animated object down to that size and overlay it onto the location.

Step 6 is where progress halted and I got stuck. Scaling a 512 drawing down to 100 pixels shrinks everything in it, so it stops matching the scene's style since the scale of everything is off, visible in my example when looking at line weight.

https://i.redd.it/w536v02c7m2i1.gif

My various workarounds to fix this:

**Generating at the object's final size**, on canvases of 128 to 320 instead of 512, so objects are generated at the size they are meant to be placed. This falls apart quickly as e.g. the same chicken comes out near-realistic at 256 or as a flat cartoon at 128 and parts get cut off or doubled. The LoRA was trained at 768 and 1024 so perhaps it's the LoRA giving out, the base model failing, or both? Would another model draw properly on small canvases and keep the lora style applied?

**The location on a bigger canvas** to combat the model degrading at smaller canvases as now the location's lines should be thinner and the objects don't have to scale so hard. However location's lines grew with it while the objects' did not. Also it would have skewed the artist's style anyway.

**Shrinking the image and generating it again at a smaller size**, img2img at denoise 0.6 to 0.8, but the redraw kept the shrunk drawing's thin lines so scale remained off. This is the one fix I really expected to work, so maybe I just set it up badly or something?

**Painting an object directly into the scene** and separating it afterwards onto white with an additional generation. Instead of generating on white and then placing, this approach basically turns it around as we place directly. This does actually fix the scale, as now the model has full reference of how an object should look in the scene, but other issues showed up like the objects being of much worse quality and partly merged with their surrounding. Also a location would need to be redrawn when objects move as mentioned earlier, but perhaps only parts could be redrawn as a workaround. This way basically solves my biggest issue of perceived scale for free so maybe this is the correct approach and I am missing something to make it work properly?

I am at the point where I want to scrap most of this and pivot to: **Pixel Art!**

Larger pixels should be able to be counted much easier, so a separate object can have the exact scale required to be placed at scale into a location. That would attempt to simplify the problem away rather than truly solving it, though perhaps that is often a good path forward. However: Does this idea even make sense, or will it break regardless? Are there perhaps other simpler existing ways to do all of this the right way?

If you're building something similar, what are you doing differently, and which tools should I go have a look at?

comments.author: Individual_Solid_944
comments.body:
I think the main issue is that you're generating each element independently, so even with the same LoRA, there's no guarantee they'll have consistent line thickness, detail density, or lighting once combined. I'd try generating the objects at roughly their intended final size rather than generating them large and scaling them down. I'd also experiment with using the actual background as a reference when generating each object, instead of relying entirely on the LoRA for style consistency.  
  
Another thing worth trying is a low-denoise img2img pass on the composed scene to unify the style, although you'd need to be careful not to alter the objects too much, especially if they're animated or need to move independently. I wouldn't switch to pixel art just to solve this. You might end up trading one set of problems for another.

comments.author: stolenyourgf
comments.body: Line weight is measured in screen pixels, so it has to be decided at the final size, it can't survive a 5x downscale. A few things that have worked for me: 1) Your inpainting route is the right one, the quality drop usually comes from inpainting a tiny area. Crop a region around the target spot, upscale that crop to the LoRA's native 1024, inpaint the object there, scale back down, then cut it out with the inpaint mask (or a segmenter like BiRefNet/SAM) for your clickable layer. 2) If you keep generating on white, pad instead of scaling: draw the object at its final size inside a full 512/1024 frame, then crop. Same resolution = same stroke width. 3) Cheap fallback: after downscaling, threshold the dark line layer and dilate it to match the background stroke width. Pixel art does simplify this, but only if the whole game uses one grid (e.g. 1 art px = 3 screen px) and objects are drawn at their pixel size, not scaled.
